items.stem: Read this from a news report, ‘Fishing Crew Rescued After 40 Hours Adrift’: ‘Five fishermen were rescued yesterday’ How many fishermen were rescued?
items.answer: Five
items.markingKey: Retrieval: the answer is stated in the quotation (‘Five fishermen were rescued yesterday’).

items.stem: In a news report, ‘Fishing Crew Rescued After 40 Hours Adrift’ the writer writes: ‘Five fishermen were rescued yesterday after spending more than 40 hours adrift in the Arabian Sea when their boat’s engine failed.’ Why is this an effective opening sentence for a news report?
items.answer: It gives the key facts at once (who, what, when, where, why) so readers grasp the story immediately; this is the ‘lead’ of an inverted pyramid.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: key facts / 5 Ws; inverted pyramid/lead

items.stem: In a news report, ‘Fishing Crew Rescued After 40 Hours Adrift’ the writer writes: ‘“When we heard the helicopter, we cried like children.”’ Why does the reporter include this quotation?
items.answer: It adds human interest and emotion, showing how desperate the men were, and the eyewitness voice makes the report vivid and credible.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: human interest/emotion; credibility/eyewitness

items.stem: Text A is a news report, ‘Fishing Crew Rescued After 40 Hours Adrift’: ‘Five fishermen were rescued yesterday after spending more than 40 hours adrift in the Arabian Sea when their boat’s engine failed. The crew of the Noor, which set out from Muscat on Monday morning, lost radio contact shortly after midday as strong winds pushed the vessel away from the coast. A coastguard helicopter spotted the boat at dawn on Wednesday, about 80 kilometres offshore. All five men were taken to hospital suffering from dehydration but are said to be in a stable condition. “We had almost given up hope,” said the captain, Salim Al-Harthy, 47. “When we heard the helicopter, we cried like children.” The coastguard has urged fishermen to carry emergency beacons, which send a satellite signal if a boat gets into difficulty.’ Text B is a feature article, ‘The Gardens in the Sky’: ‘Seven floors above the traffic of downtown Singapore, Mei Lim is picking chillies. Around her, in raised beds made from recycled crates, grow tomatoes, aubergines, lemongrass and a tangle of beans that has climbed halfway up the lift shaft. “People think you need a field to grow food,” she laughs, wiping soil from her hands. “You just need a roof and a bit of stubbornness.” Mei is one of a growing number of city dwellers turning unused rooftops into farms. Supporters say the gardens cool buildings, cut food miles and give neighbours a reason to talk to each other. Critics point out that they will never feed a whole city. But up here, with bees drifting between the flowers and the city humming below, it is hard not to feel that something important is taking root.’ Explain how Text A shows the features of a news report and Text B the features of a feature article.
items.answer: Text A: lead with 5 Ws; past tense; third person; facts and figures; quotations; inverted pyramid with background last. Text B: present-tense scene-setting opening; personal angle (Mei); descriptive detail; quotations for personality; both sides discussed; reflective, witty ending (pun).
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 per valid feature with evidence, from both texts; credit comparison of purpose (inform quickly vs explore and engage).

items.stem: Identify the feature of a newspaper text shown here, explain its purpose, and write your own example of the same feature for a story about a school sports day: ‘The coastguard has urged fishermen to carry emergency beacons, which send a satellite signal if a boat gets into difficulty.’
items.answer: Inverted pyramid: background advice comes last because it is least essential. Own example: any accurate inverted pyramid about a sports day.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: 1 for inverted pyramid; 1 for purpose; remaining mark(s) for an accurate original example.

items.stem: Write a news report for students in a school magazine using these notes. You may add realistic details. items.stem: Analyse how the writer uses language in these two quotations from a feature article, ‘The Gardens in the Sky’: (i) ‘“You just need a roof and a bit of stubbornness.”’ (ii) ‘with bees drifting between the flowers and the city humming below’ Identify a technique in each and explain its effect.

items.stem: Read a persuasive article from a school magazine, ‘Ditch the Plastic Bottle’: ‘Every day, our school throws away more than four hundred plastic bottles. Four hundred! Imagine them piled in the playground: a glittering mountain of waste that will outlive every one of us. Is that really the legacy we want to leave? Some people say that recycling solves the problem, but only a small fraction of all the plastic ever made has been recycled. The rest is buried, burned or washed into the sea, where it chokes turtles and breaks down into tiny fragments that end up in the fish we eat. The solution is simple, cheap and fair: install free water fountains and give every student a refillable bottle. Other schools in our city have already done it. items.stem: Write the script of a two-minute presentation to your class about a technology that has changed the way we live, then write a short reflection on how you would make it engaging when you speak. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model: hook (question or striking fact); three signposted points about a technology that has changed the way we live; conclusion with call to action; reflection on delivery (pauses, eye contact, key-word slides).
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 6 marks, Style and accuracy 4 marks. Content and structure – top band (5–6): a clear purpose and point of view; strong, consistent sense of audience; rhetorical devices used purposefully; well-signposted structure with an effective opening and ending; middle band (3–4): clear purpose with some awareness of audience; some rhetorical devices; structure mostly clear; lower band (1–2): purpose unclear; little sense of a listening audience; few devices; loosely organised. Style and accuracy – top band (3–4): precise, often ambitious vocabulary chosen for effect; a wide range of sentence structures used deliberately; register consistently suited to audience and purpose; spelling, punctuation and grammar almost always accurate; middle band (2): generally appropriate vocabulary with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly suitable; occasional errors that do not obscure meaning; lower band (1): simple or repetitive vocabulary; limited sentence variety; register may slip; frequent errors in spelling, punctuation or grammar that sometimes obscure meaning. Indicative content: script with greeting, hook, signposted points, evidence, conclusion; reflection on voice, pace, pauses, eye contact, visual aids.

items.stem: Read this from a news report, ‘Fishing Crew Rescued After 40 Hours Adrift’: ‘All five men were taken to hospital suffering from dehydration’ What were the men suffering from?
items.answer: Dehydration
items.markingKey: Retrieval: the answer is stated in the quotation (‘All five men were taken to hospital suffering from dehydration’).

items.stem: In a feature article, ‘The Gardens in the Sky’ the writer writes: ‘Supporters say the gardens cool buildings, cut food miles and give neighbours a reason to talk to each other. Critics point out that they will never feed a whole city.’ How does the writer show balance here?
items.answer: Benefits from supporters are followed by a criticism, so both views are presented before the writer’s own closing judgement.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: both sides; reference to ‘Supporters say’/‘Critics point out’

items.stem: Text A is a news report, ‘Student’s Microplastic Filter Wins Top Prize’: ‘A 15-year-old from Nairobi has won first prize at an international young scientists” competition for a low-cost filter that traps microplastics in washing-machine water. Wanjiru Kamau’s device, built from recycled bottles and layers of cotton mesh, captured up to 80 per cent of plastic fibres in tests at her school laboratory. Tiny fibres shed from synthetic clothes are among the most common forms of plastic pollution in rivers and oceans. “I kept seeing the river near my home getting dirtier,” Wanjiru said. “I wanted to stop the problem before it reached the water.” The judges praised the invention as “simple, cheap and genuinely useful”. Wanjiru will receive $5,000 towards her studies and plans to share the design online so that other schools can build their own.’ Text B is a feature article, ‘The Gardens in the Sky’: ‘Seven floors above the traffic of downtown Singapore, Mei Lim is picking chillies. Around her, in raised beds made from recycled crates, grow tomatoes, aubergines, lemongrass and a tangle of beans that has climbed halfway up the lift shaft. “People think you need a field to grow food,” she laughs, wiping soil from her hands. “You just need a roof and a bit of stubbornness.” Mei is one of a growing number of city dwellers turning unused rooftops into farms. Supporters say the gardens cool buildings, cut food miles and give neighbours a reason to talk to each other. Critics point out that they will never feed a whole city. But up here, with bees drifting between the flowers and the city humming below, it is hard not to feel that something important is taking root.’ Explain how Text A shows the features of a news report and Text B the features of a feature article.
items.answer: Text A: lead with 5 Ws; past tense; third person; facts and figures; quotations; inverted pyramid with background last. Text B: present-tense scene-setting opening; personal angle (Mei); descriptive detail; quotations for personality; both sides discussed; reflective, witty ending (pun).
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 per valid feature with evidence, from both texts; credit comparison of purpose (inform quickly vs explore and engage).

items.stem: Write an online news article with a headline and a subheading for residents of a city using these notes. You may add realistic details. Notes: Sunday; first car-free day in city centre; 10 a.m.–4 p.m.; streets used for cycling, music, food stalls; around 15,000 visitors; air pollution down 30% on the day (city monitoring); some shop owners report fewer sales; mayor plans monthly car-free days. Write about 350–450 words.
items.answer: Model structure: headline; lead with 5 Ws; details in order of importance; quotation(s) integrated with reporting verbs; background and next steps last; objective tone adapted to the audience.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 12: Content and structure 7 marks, Style and accuracy 5 marks. Content and structure – top band (5–7): all key facts (who, what, where, when, why, how) in an effective lead; inverted-pyramid structure; quotations used well; objective tone and a headline suited to the audience; middle band (3–4): most key facts covered; recognisable report structure; some quotation; tone mostly objective; lower band (1–2): facts incomplete or disordered; little sense of report form; tone personal or inconsistent. Style and accuracy – top band (4–5): precise, often ambitious vocabulary chosen for effect; a wide range of sentence structures used deliberately; register consistently suited to audience and purpose; spelling, punctuation and grammar almost always accurate; middle band (2–3): generally appropriate vocabulary with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly suitable; occasional errors that do not obscure meaning; lower band (1): simple or repetitive vocabulary; limited sentence variety; register may slip; frequent errors in spelling, punctuation or grammar that sometimes obscure meaning. Indicative content: all key facts from the notes; correct order; quotation punctuated; register suited to residents of a city.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Why do newspapers often use puns in headlines? (b) Which structural choice most influences what readers think is important?
items.answer: (a) To make the headline witty and memorable and attract readers (b) The order in which information is presented
items.markingKey: (a) Puns entertain and catch the eye. (b) Writers put what they want emphasised first or last.

items.stem: The headline ‘Fury Over Bus Fare Hike’ uses emotive language. Explain how it is designed to influence readers.
items.answer: Emotive language: ‘Fury’ suggests strong public anger and grabs attention.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for identifying emotive language; further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: ‘Fury’ suggests strong public anger and grabs attention.

items.stem: Analyse how this headline tries to attract and influence readers: ‘Tiny Hands, Giant Hearts: Pupils Raise $10,000’ Then write an alternative headline for the same story using a different technique.
items.answer: Contrast: opposites (tiny/giant) highlight the achievement. Alternative: any accurate headline using a different technique (e.g. a question, alliteration or a pun).
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for contrast; 1 for effect; remaining mark(s) for an effective alternative using a named technique.

items.stem: Read a news report, ‘Student’s Microplastic Filter Wins Top Prize’: ‘A 15-year-old from Nairobi has won first prize at an international young scientists” competition for a low-cost filter that traps microplastics in washing-machine water. Wanjiru Kamau’s device, built from recycled bottles and layers of cotton mesh, captured up to 80 per cent of plastic fibres in tests at her school laboratory. Tiny fibres shed from synthetic clothes are among the most common forms of plastic pollution in rivers and oceans. “I kept seeing the river near my home getting dirtier,” Wanjiru said. “I wanted to stop the problem before it reached the water.” The judges praised the invention as “simple, cheap and genuinely useful”. Wanjiru will receive $5,000 towards her studies and plans to share the design online so that other schools can build their own.’ Explain how the order of information makes readers admire Wanjiru.
items.answer: Achievement first; details of the invention and impressive figure (80%); background on why it matters; her personal motive in her own words; judges’ praise; generous plan to share the design last.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: 1 per valid structural point (opening, order, placement of quotation, ending) linked to its effect on readers.

items.stem: Read a news report, ‘Student’s Microplastic Filter Wins Top Prize’: ‘A 15-year-old from Nairobi has won first prize at an international young scientists” competition for a low-cost filter that traps microplastics in washing-machine water. Wanjiru Kamau’s device, built from recycled bottles and layers of cotton mesh, captured up to 80 per cent of plastic fibres in tests at her school laboratory. Tiny fibres shed from synthetic clothes are among the most common forms of plastic pollution in rivers and oceans. “I kept seeing the river near my home getting dirtier,” Wanjiru said. “I wanted to stop the problem before it reached the water.” The judges praised the invention as “simple, cheap and genuinely useful”. Wanjiru will receive $5,000 towards her studies and plans to share the design online so that other schools can build their own.’ How does the writer use language and structure to influence the reader’s view of the people and events?
items.answer: Word choice and connotations; use and placement of quotations; facts and figures; opening and ending; balance or bias; overall effect on readers’ attitudes.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10 (reading). Top band (7–10): perceptive, well-developed analysis of how the writer uses language and structure to create effects; precise, well-chosen references; sustained focus on the question; middle band (4–6): clear explanation of some effects with relevant references; some analysis of particular words and phrases; lower band (1–3): some relevant points, mostly retelling the text; few references; little comment on language. Indicative content: Word choice and connotations; use and placement of quotations; facts and figures; opening and ending; balance or bias; overall effect on readers’ attitudes.

items.stem: A reporter is writing for residents of the town from these notes: Notes: Tuesday night; storm; 120 mm rain in 6 hours; River Kalu burst banks; 40 homes flooded in Lower Town; no injuries; school used as shelter; council leader: “Our volunteers worked all night”; clean-up starts Thursday; flood barrier plan delayed since 2019. Which piece of information would you put in the final paragraph, and why?
items.answer: The least important or background information (e.g. future plans or wider context) goes last, following the inverted pyramid; the quotation “Our volunteers worked all night” could go near the end for human interest.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: sensible choice of background/future information; reason linked to the inverted pyramid.

items.stem: A reporter is writing for local students from these notes: Notes: Saturday; Riverside School robotics team (4 students, aged 13–14); won national schools robotics final in Kuala Lumpur; robot sorts recycling; beat 32 teams; captain Aisha Rahman: “We failed three times before it worked”; prize: trip to world championships in Tokyo. Which piece of information would you put in the final paragraph, and why?
items.answer: The least important or background information (e.g. future plans or wider context) goes last, following the inverted pyramid; the quotation “We failed three times before it worked” could go near the end for human interest.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: sensible choice of background/future information; reason linked to the inverted pyramid.

items.stem: Use these notes to write a headline and an opening paragraph (lead) for a news report aimed at readers of a local newspaper. Notes: Monday; fire at a bakery on Market Street, 5 a.m.; baker Mr Osei escaped unharmed; neighbours raised $8,000 online in two days to rebuild; fire caused by an electrical fault; reopening planned in two months; Mr Osei: “I have never felt so loved by this street.”
items.answer: Model: a short, striking headline; a lead of one or two sentences answering who, what, where, when and why, in the past tense and third person, with language suited to the audience.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for an effective headline; 1–2 for covering the 5 Ws accurately; 1 for register suited to readers of a local newspaper.

items.stem: Read this transcript from a student’s spoken contribution: ‘Um, so, my presentation is about, um, recycling. Recycling is good. It is good because, um, it is good for the planet. That is it.’ Evaluate one strength or weakness of this contribution and explain its effect on listeners.
items.answer: Weaknesses: fillers (um), no clear structure, repetition of ‘good’, no evidence, abrupt ending. Strengths: topic is stated.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for an accurate strength/weakness; 1 for its effect on listeners; a further mark for supporting reference.

items.stem: Read this transcript: ‘Um, so, my presentation is about, um, recycling. Recycling is good. It is good because, um, it is good for the planet. That is it.’ Write feedback for the speaker giving one strength, one weakness and two specific improvements, with reasons.
items.answer: Weaknesses: fillers (um), no clear structure, repetition of ‘good’, no evidence, abrupt ending. Strengths: topic is stated. Improvements: Plan a hook, three points with evidence and a conclusion; replace fillers with pauses; vary vocabulary.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: valid strength; valid weakness; two specific, practical improvements; reasons linked to the audience.
